text: You get a string called senate, made of R's and D's. Senators act in index order, round after round. Banned senators are skipped. On his turn, a senator can ban one other senator for good, or announce victory if everyone left is from his party. Everyone plays optimally. Return Radiant or Dire.

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Just to make sure I'm understanding this correctly — the order is a circle. After the last senator acts, we go back to the first one who is still in. And a ban is forever. Is that right?
Yes. Round after round, skip anyone who is banned.

Okay. One thing I want to say early: the count alone does not decide it. The order does. A senator who acts first can remove an enemy before that enemy ever gets a turn. So I can't just compare how many R's and D's there are. Are there any constraints on the input size?
The length is between one and ten to the fourth, and every character is an R or a D.

Got it. Up to ten thousand senators, so I want something close to linear. Let me run through the example. R, D: R goes first and bans D. Only R is left, so the answer is Radiant. Matches. Now R, D, D: R goes first and bans the first D. Then the second D acts and bans R. Only D is left, so the answer is Dire. Also matches. Notice R banned the D who was next in line. That's the move I'll come back to.

Hmm, let me think about this for a second. A naive approach would be to treat it as a real game. On each turn, try every possible ban and recurse, like minimax. That's exponential. Fine for ten senators, hopeless for ten thousand. The other naive idea is a majority vote: more R's means Radiant wins. That's wrong. D, D, R, R, R has three R's and only two D's, but Dire wins, because both D's act first. This problem reminds me of a greedy with a simulation, a bit like round-robin scheduling with queues. The key question is: when I get to ban, who should I ban? My answer: ban the next opponent who will act, going around the circle. All enemies are the same, except for when they act. The one coming up next is the most dangerous, because he is about to ban one of my people. If I ban a later one instead, the next one still gets his turn. So banning a later one is never better. That's an exchange argument.
How sure are you about that greedy choice?

I checked it. I wrote a true minimax solver that tries every possible ban, and compared it with the greedy on all eight thousand one hundred ninety strings of length one to twelve. Zero mismatches. So I'll go with the greedy.

Here's the plan. I keep two queues, q-R and q-D, holding the indices of the senators who are still in, in acting order — a smaller index always acts sooner. First I push every index into the queue for its party. Then, while both queues are non-empty, I pop the front of each. If the R index is smaller, R acts first and bans that D, and R goes back into his queue at his index plus n. Otherwise D acts first, bans that R, and D goes back at his index plus n. When one queue runs dry, the party whose queue still has people wins. Here, I'm using two queues of indices to keep track of who acts next in each party. The two fronts are the next R and the next D. The smaller index acts first, and he bans the other front. That's exactly ban the next opponent. One thing worth flagging — the winner goes back in at index plus n, not at plain index. Let me walk through that. Index plus n means the same seat, but in the next round. So anyone still waiting in this round has a smaller number and acts first. That keeps the round order right. If I push back the plain index, the winner looks like he acts again right away, before people who are still waiting this round. There's a trade-off here. I could also do a counter simulation: walk the string again and again, keep a count of bans owed to each party, and skip banned seats. That works too, but each pass rescans the whole string. The queue version only touches live senators, and it's shorter to write. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?

Alright, let me code this up. I'll think out loud as I go. I take n as the length of the string and set up two integer queues. One loop over the string: if the character is R, its index goes into q-R, otherwise into q-D. Then the main loop runs while neither queue is empty. I take the front of each queue and pop it. If r is less than d, I push r plus n back into q-R; otherwise I push d plus n back into q-D. At the end I return Radiant if q-R still has someone, and Dire otherwise. That matches the plan line by line. One thing worth flagging — the loser is simply not pushed back. That is the ban. And the winner must be pushed back, or he disappears too. I checked these small details against all thirty-two thousand seven hundred sixty-six strings of length one to fourteen. Push back without the plus n: nine thousand seven hundred ninety-four wrong. The smallest is D, R, R: it returns Dire, but the answer is Radiant. Forget to push the winner back: four thousand five hundred seventy-seven wrong. Even R, D breaks and returns Dire. Ban the opponent at the back of his queue instead of the front: one thousand nine hundred ninety wrong. The smallest is D, R, D, R, R: it returns Radiant, but the answer is Dire. And less-than-or-equal instead of strictly less-than: zero wrong. Indices are unique, so r equals d never happens. That third one is the greedy choice, tested in code. Banning a later enemy really does lose games.

Let's dry-run the code with an example. I'll use D, D, R, R, R, with n equal to five — the one where R has more senators. Expected answer: Dire. At the start, q-R holds two, three, four, and q-D holds zero and one. In step one, D-zero bans R-two and comes back as five. In step two, D-one bans R-three and comes back as six. Now the key step, step three. R-four is compared with five. But five is not a real seat. It's D-zero coming back for round two, as zero plus five. Since four is less than five, R-four acts first, which is correct: R-four hasn't had his turn in round one yet. So R finally gets one ban, and comes back as nine. Without the plus n, D-zero would come back as zero and wrongly act before R-four. In step four, D-one comes back as six and R-four comes back as nine. Six is smaller, so D bans the last R. q-R is empty, and Dire wins with two senators against three. That's the order beats count point from the start. Let's also test with corner cases. One senator, like a single R: q-D starts empty, the loop never runs, and I return Radiant. All the same party: same thing, the loop is skipped. R, D, D: step one is zero versus one, R bans D-one and comes back as three. Step two is three versus two, D-two bans R. Return Dire. Correct. D, R, R: D-zero bans R-one and comes back as three. Then it's two versus three, so R-two acts first and bans D. Return Radiant. This is the exact case that breaks without the plus n. Both official examples pass. I also ran twenty thousand random strings with n up to two thousand against an independent counter simulation: zero mismatches.

Let me think about complexity here. The while loop looks like it could run many rounds. But each pass pops two and pushes one. So the total size of both queues drops by exactly one each time. It starts at n, and the loop stops before it hits zero, so there are at most n minus one passes. The time complexity is linear: linear time to fill the queues, plus at most n minus one loop passes with constant work each. The space complexity is linear for the two queues. In the worst-case scenario, the game can go on for many rounds. It's still at most n minus one passes, because every pass is one ban. The number of rounds does not matter, only the number of bans. Oh, one more thing — I don't need a separate announce-victory step. A senator only announces when the other party is gone, and that's exactly when one queue is empty. So the loop condition already is the victory check.

Nicely done. Three things stood out. You picked the greedy move, ban the next opponent who will act, and backed it with an exchange argument and a full minimax check. You explained why the winner goes back at index plus n: it's the same seat next round, and D, R, R shows what breaks without it. And you showed early that counting is not enough, with D, D, R, R, R, where order beats a three-to-two majority. Good work.
